slides.punch: Four things they filed. None made the headline.
slides.why: Marvell reported Tuesday: revenue up 37%, a beat, guidance raised again. The stock fell 10% the very next session. That gap between the headline and the tape is where these four things live — buried in the notes to a 10-Q filed three months ago, not in Tuesday's press release. We take each one in turn.
slides.notes: COLD OPEN, to camera before the deck: Marvell just beat every single number on its earnings report and raised its outlook again — and the stock fell double digits today anyway. That does not make sense until you read what is actually in the filings. Four things buried in the 10-Q and the fine print explain what the headline beat does not. THEN the slide: here they are. TARGET 24s.

slides.punch: GAAP EPS is 35% of non-GAAP. That gap is not just stock comp.

Sitting right next to it, almost unremarked: what Marvell actually earned under standard accounting rules was only $0.33 a share. Stock handed to employees explains some of that gap. It does not explain all of it — there's a second item in there, and we're about to find it.
slides.notes: First, the quarter as reported yesterday after the close. Revenue two point seven three nine billion, a record, up thirty seven percent year over year. Non-GAAP earnings ninety four cents a share, comfortably ahead of estimates. But look at the GAAP number right next to it: thirty three cents. Less than half. That gap is not just stock comp — there's something else in there, and we're about to find it. TARGET 24s.

slides.head: The biggest beat. The worst reaction.
slides.sub: Each dot: the next session's move. The label: the beat size.
slides.punch: This was the biggest beat in six quarters. The stock fell anyway.
slides.why: Marvell has beaten its own guidance midpoint every single quarter shown here — anywhere from $6.0M to $20.0M in the six quarters between Q3'25's outsized beat and today, and by $39.0M today, comfortably the biggest of that run. None of that predicts the reaction. Reactions here span from −20% to +23%, with no relationship to beat size at all. What actually moved the stock today was three lines down in the outlook: Q3's guided margin, which came in below what the company just delivered.
slides.notes: Finding one. Marvell's stock does not trade on whether it beats guidance — it always beats guidance, by a little, like clockwork. Every single quarter for the last eight has landed above the midpoint the company set three months earlier. Today's beat, thirty nine million dollars, was the biggest of the last seven quarters. And the stock still fell more than ten percent. Look at the pattern across two years: reactions ranging from plus twenty three percent to minus twenty percent, with no relationship at all to how big the beat was. What actually moved it today was three lines down in the outlook: next quarter's margin guide, which came in below what the company just delivered. TARGET 30s.

slides.punch: $303M of GAAP earnings, spent managing Marvell's own earnout exposure.
slides.why: Marvell paid $3.5B for a company called Celestial AI — more than half in stock, not cash. Part of the payment is a bonus tied to future results, calculated using Marvell's OWN share price. So when the stock jumps on unrelated AI news, this bonus liability jumps too — it grew from $316M to $648M in one quarter, and Marvell had to buy a hedge on its own shares just to manage it. That's not money spent on chips or engineers. It's $303M spent managing a problem Marvell created for itself.
slides.notes: Finding three, and this is the one that explains the GAAP-to-non-GAAP gap from the scoreboard slide. In February, Marvell paid three and a half billion dollars for a company called Celestial AI — fifty five percent of it in stock, twenty four and a half million new shares. Celestial's revenue so far: the filing's own words, 'not material.' But here's the part nobody flagged: part of that deal is an earnout, and its accounting value is modeled off Marvell's OWN stock price. As the stock ran up on AI headlines this year, that liability swelled — three hundred two million dollars of GAAP earnings drag in just two quarters, net of a hedge Marvell had to go buy specifically to manage the exposure it created. That's real money spent managing an accounting mechanism, not the business. TARGET 32s.

It is sitting on a strategic equity stake that is already deeply in the money, and almost nothing written about this earnings report mentioned it.

slides.punch: $48.1M sold. The only buying was a payroll-deduction plan.
slides.why: Recomputed from every Form 4 Marvell's executives filed over 16 months — no single filing adds this up. Seven people sold a combined $48.1M, led by the Data Center president, the CEO, and the COO. Most of it — 79% of the sale filings — was set up months in advance, not a same-day call. The exception: the brand-new CFO sold shares just eight days into the job, with no such plan on file. And the only buying in that whole window was one routine payroll-deduction purchase, not a person deciding to buy.
slides.notes: One more thing, and it took the most digging of anything in this episode: every Form 4 Marvell's executives and directors have filed in the last sixteen months, re-parsed by hand because no single filing adds this up. Seven people sold stock — the CEO, the COO, the Data Center president, the general counsel, and both the outgoing and incoming CFO — forty eight million dollars combined. Most of it, about eighty percent, was on a pre-set trading plan scheduled months ahead, which is the fair, boring explanation for most insider selling. But one sale wasn't on any plan: the brand new CFO, eight days into the job, sold shares with no 10b5-1 plan cited anywhere in the filing. And here's the part that actually surprised me: in sixteen months, the only shares anyone bought were twenty seven thousand two hundred shares, picked up by four executives on the exact same day, at the exact same price — a routine paycheck stock-purchase plan, not a single person deciding this was a good time to buy. Seven sellers. Zero real buyers. TARGET 32s.

slides.head: Cheaper than Broadcom. Growing slower too.
slides.sub: Market value against the latest quarter annualized, growth beside.
slides.punch: 0.9× Broadcom’s multiple, but growing 11 points slower.
slides.why: Same yardstick for everyone here: what the market pays for each dollar of a company's sales. Against Broadcom — the closest direct comparison in custom AI silicon — Marvell costs about 88 cents on the dollar. That looks cheap until you check growth: Marvell's revenue grew 37% against Broadcom's 48%. An 11-point growth gap on a roughly 12% cheaper price tag is not automatically a bargain — the two look closer once you weigh in how fast each one is growing.
slides.notes: So what are you paying for this? Same yardstick for everyone: market value against the latest reported quarter, annualized, growth right beside it. Against Broadcom — the closest direct comparison in custom AI silicon — Marvell trades at a real discount per dollar of sales. But check growth before you call that cheap: Marvell is growing meaningfully slower than Broadcom right now. A real discount, against a real growth gap — on a growth-adjusted basis the two are closer than the sticker price alone suggests. TARGET 24s.

verdict.callLine: The Data Center growth is real. So is the earnout tax on every AI headline this stock trades on.

tiles.fact: Data Center revenue up 46% YoY, guided to accelerate further into Q3
Three of the last four earnings prints moved the stock more than 10% in a single session, in both directions
GAAP EPS ran 65% below non-GAAP EPS this quarter, largely stock comp and an earnout tied to Marvell's own share price
79% of revenue is now Data Center; Communications and other shrank sequentially
Net debt is a modest $1.0B against $18.5B of equity, but goodwill jumped $2.8B in one quarter on a stock-funded deal
Priced between my base and bull cases after today's drop

scored.fact: Data Center +46% YoY, guided to accelerate
GAAP EPS diluted by a self-referential earnout
One segment carries the whole story
Low net leverage, but goodwill-heavy after Celestial
Between base and bull after today's selloff

working: Data Center revenue is genuinely accelerating — 46% year-over-year, 18% sequentially, and management guided Q3 revenue to $3.15B, another double-digit sequential step up.
NVIDIA put $2.0B of real money into Marvell as a strategic investor, not just a customer, via convertible preferred stock struck well below today's price.
Net leverage is low — about $1.0B of net debt against $18.5B of stockholders' equity — and every senior note is laddered years out with no near-term maturity wall.
There is a real, dated catalyst ahead: management's own Investor Day on October 6, 2026, where it plans to lay out the long-term AI infrastructure strategy in detail.
Every quarter for at least two years has beaten its own guidance midpoint — the execution track record on the number the company controls is intact.
watch: Q3 FY27's guided non-GAAP gross margin (57.5%-58.5%) sits below Q2's actual 58.9% — margin, not revenue, is what actually moved the stock today.
The Celestial earnout is a bet on Marvell's own stock price, not on Celestial's business — 'not material' revenue so far, and a liability that grows precisely when the stock does.
Communications and other revenue fell 3% sequentially even as Data Center masked it — a second data point here and this becomes a real crack, not a rounding error.
Distributor A now accounts for 37% of net revenue, up from 24% two fiscal years ago — a concentration that keeps climbing.

Seven executives have sold $48.1M combined over 16 months and bought nothing on their own initiative — most on pre-set plans, but that is a lot of one-way conviction from the people who see the numbers first.
why: The growth is concentrated but real. Data Center is 79% of Marvell now and it is the only segment actually accelerating — that is a legitimate AI-infrastructure story, not a headline.

The earnings quality has a self-inflicted wound. A $3.5B acquisition structured with a stock-price-linked earnout has already cost $302.7M of GAAP earnings in two quarters — money spent managing an accounting exposure the company created by how it wrote the deal.
The price already needs a lot to go right. At $216.70 the stock sits between my base and bull cases — today's drop bought you a slightly better entry, not a cheap one.
A decent price for me: $210.59 or lower. That is roughly the midpoint of a model that already assumes Data Center keeps compounding — near it or below, the odds start working for you.
